cards.front: What is the inguinal canal and how long is it?
cards.back: An oblique intermuscular slit about 4 cm long in the lower part of the anterior abdominal wall, running just above and parallel to the medial half of the inguinal ligament.

cards.front: What is the developmental reason for the existence of the inguinal canal?
cards.back: It is the track along which the testis descends from the posterior abdominal wall into the scrotum, dragging its coverings, vessels and duct with it; in the female it transmits the round ligament to the labium majus.

cards.front: In which direction does the inguinal canal run?
cards.back: Downwards, forwards and medially, from the deep ring laterally to the superficial ring medially.

cards.front: What forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal?
cards.back: The external oblique aponeurosis along the whole length of the canal, reinforced laterally by the fleshy fibres of the internal oblique.

cards.front: What forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal?
cards.back: The fascia transversalis along the whole length, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.

cards.front: What forms the roof of the inguinal canal?
cards.back: The arching lowest fibres of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis as they pass from the inguinal ligament to the conjoint tendon.

cards.front: What forms the floor of the inguinal canal?
cards.back: The in-rolled lower border of the inguinal ligament, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament.

cards.front: Which wall is reinforced in front of the deep ring, and which behind the superficial ring?
cards.back: The internal oblique reinforces the anterior wall in front of the deep ring; the conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall behind the superficial ring. The two weak points are therefore never opposite a weak wall.

cards.front: What are the contents of the inguinal canal in the male?
cards.back: The spermatic cord and the ilioinguinal nerve, which lies outside the cord coverings on its anterolateral surface.

cards.front: What are the contents of the inguinal canal in the female?
cards.back: The round ligament of the uterus with its accompanying artery, and the ilioinguinal nerve.

cards.front: Which nerve traverses the canal without entering through the deep ring?
cards.back: The ilioinguinal nerve. It pierces the internal oblique to enter the canal from its lateral side and leaves through the superficial ring.

cards.front: List the mechanisms that protect the inguinal canal.
cards.back: Obliquity of the canal so the two rings are not opposite each other, the shutter mechanism of the arching internal oblique and transversus fibres, the ball-valve action of the cremaster, the slit-valve action of the external oblique on the superficial ring, and the flap-valve effect of intra-abdominal pressure pressing the posterior wall against the anterior wall.

cards.front: Describe the shutter mechanism.
cards.back: When the abdominal muscles contract, the arched lower fibres of the internal oblique and transversus straighten and descend towards the inguinal ligament, closing the canal like a shutter against the rising intra-abdominal pressure.

cards.front: How does the cremaster contribute to canal protection?
cards.back: On contraction it pulls the cord upwards and laterally so that the bulk of the cord plugs the superficial ring - the ball-valve action.

cards.front: Why does a wide or attenuated superficial ring not by itself cause a hernia?
cards.back: The hernia arises at a defect in the deep ring or the posterior wall. A wide superficial ring only permits an existing sac to emerge, which is why repair is directed at the posterior wall and the deep ring.

cards.front: What is the deep inguinal ring?
cards.back: An oval opening in the fascia transversalis, the mouth of the funnel that becomes the internal spermatic fascia. It is the entry point of the canal.

cards.front: Where does the department place the deep inguinal ring?
cards.back: About half an inch (1.25 cm) above the mid-inguinal point, and just above the femoral artery pulsation.

cards.front: Distinguish the mid-inguinal point from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.
cards.back: The mid-inguinal point is midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis and overlies the femoral artery. The midpoint of the inguinal ligament is midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle and lies just below the deep ring.

cards.front: What is the immediate medial relation of the deep inguinal ring?
cards.back: The inferior epigastric vessels, which is the anatomical landmark used to separate an indirect from a direct hernia.

cards.front: What is the superficial inguinal ring?
cards.back: A triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis lying above and medial to the pubic tubercle, the exit of the canal.

cards.front: Name the boundaries of the superficial inguinal ring.
cards.back: The medial and lateral crura of the external oblique aponeurosis at the sides, the intercrural fibres above and laterally, and the pubic crest at the base.

cards.front: Which layer of the cord is acquired at the superficial ring?
cards.back: The external spermatic fascia, derived from the external oblique aponeurosis.

cards.front: Give the boundaries of Hesselbach's triangle as used in surgery.
cards.back: Medially the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, laterally the inferior epigastric artery, and inferiorly the inguinal ligament.

cards.front: What is the floor of Hesselbach's triangle?
cards.back: The fascia transversalis reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon - the medial part of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

cards.front: Which hernia passes through Hesselbach's triangle?
cards.back: A direct inguinal hernia, which pushes straight forwards through the posterior wall medial to the inferior epigastric artery.

cards.front: How does the myopectineal orifice of Fruchaud unify groin hernias?
cards.back: It is the single fascial window bounded above by the arch of internal oblique and transversus, medially by the rectus, laterally by iliopsoas and below by the pecten pubis, crossed by the inguinal ligament. Every direct, indirect and femoral hernia passes through it, which is why a single preperitoneal mesh covering it repairs all three.

cards.front: List the three arteries of the spermatic cord.
cards.back: The testicular artery from the aorta, the artery to the vas (cremasteric branch of the inferior vesical artery) and the cremasteric artery from the inferior epigastric artery.

cards.front: List the three nerves related to the spermatic cord.
cards.back: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplying cremaster, sympathetic fibres from the testicular plexus, and the ilioinguinal nerve which lies on the cord rather than within it.

cards.front: List the remaining contents of the spermatic cord.
cards.back: The vas deferens, the pampiniform plexus of veins, lymphatics of the testis, and the remains of the processus vaginalis.

cards.front: Name the three coverings of the spermatic cord and the layer each is derived from.
cards.back: External spermatic fascia from the external oblique aponeurosis, cremasteric muscle and fascia from the internal oblique, and internal spermatic fascia from the fascia transversalis.

cards.front: Why does the cord have no covering derived from transversus abdominis?
cards.back: The cord passes beneath the arching lower border of transversus abdominis rather than through it, so that muscle contributes no covering.

cards.front: What are the coverings of an oblique inguinal hernia while it lies in the inguinal region?
cards.back: Skin, superficial fascia, external oblique aponeurosis, then the cremasteric muscle and fascia and the internal spermatic fascia.

cards.front: What are the coverings of the same hernia once it has reached the scrotum?
cards.back: Skin, non-fatty superficial fascia containing the dartos muscle, then the three cord coverings - external spermatic fascia, cremasteric muscle and fascia and internal spermatic fascia.

cards.front: How is the hernial sac recognised at operation?
cards.back: By its opaque pearly white colour, definite edges and crescentic fundus, and by its position anterolateral to the vas and vessels within the cord.

cards.front: How is the neck of the sac identified?
cards.back: It is the narrowest part of the sac, it lies at the level of the extraperitoneal fat, and the inferior epigastric vessels lie on its medial side.

cards.front: Why must the sac be dissected to its neck before ligation?
cards.back: A ligature applied short of the neck leaves a residual peritoneal pouch that will refill and recur. Transfixion at the neck lets the stump retract flush with the parietal peritoneum.

cards.front: What are the relations of the vas deferens at the deep ring?
cards.back: It hooks around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery to turn medially into the pelvis, crossing the external iliac vessels, and it lies posteromedial to the other cord structures.

cards.front: Which nerves are at risk in an open inguinal hernia repair?
cards.back: The ilioinguinal nerve on the cord, the iliohypogastric nerve above it, and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve entering with the cord at the deep ring. Entrapment of any of them causes chronic inguinodynia.

cards.front: Define the anatomical course of an oblique (indirect) inguinal hernia.
cards.back: The sac enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, travels down the whole length of the canal inside the cord coverings, and may emerge from the superficial ring into the scrotum.

cards.front: Where does the sac of an oblique inguinal hernia lie in relation to the vas and vessels?
cards.back: Always anterolateral to them, inside the cord coverings.

cards.front: Define the anatomical course of a direct inguinal hernia.
cards.back: The sac bulges directly forwards through the weakened fascia transversalis of Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, and lies outside the cord coverings behind the cord.

cards.front: Why does a direct hernia rarely strangulate?
cards.back: It has a wide neck and a broad diffuse defect, so its contents move in and out freely; strangulation requires a narrow constricting ring.

cards.front: Why does a direct hernia rarely reach the scrotum?
cards.back: It does not travel along the canal but pushes forwards through the posterior wall, and the superficial ring and the intact external oblique limit its descent.

cards.front: Distinguish a congenital from an acquired sac in an oblique inguinal hernia.
cards.back: A congenital or preformed sac is an unobliterated processus vaginalis. An acquired or pulsion sac is formed by peritoneum pushed out by raised intra-abdominal pressure through a weak deep ring.

cards.front: Describe the congenital anatomical type of oblique inguinal hernia.
cards.back: The whole processus vaginalis persists, so the hernia reaches the bottom of the scrotum and the testis lies among the contents of the sac.

cards.front: Describe the infantile type of oblique inguinal hernia.
cards.back: The tunica vaginalis extends upwards to the superficial ring and the sac descends behind it, so at operation two sacs are found and the tunica may be opened by mistake.

cards.front: What is a bubonocele?
cards.back: An adult-type oblique hernia limited to the inguinal canal, the processus vaginalis being obliterated at the superficial ring, presenting as a groin bulge only.

cards.front: What is a funicular hernia?
cards.back: An adult type in which the processus is closed only at its lower end just above the epididymis; the hernia reaches the neck of the scrotum and the testis can be felt separately below it.

cards.front: What is a complete or scrotal hernia?
cards.back: An adult-type hernia that descends to the bottom of the scrotum; the testis lies behind the hernia and is difficult to define but is still separate from the contents.

cards.front: State the pubic tubercle rule that separates an inguinal from a femoral hernia.
cards.back: An inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle; a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to it.

cards.front: Describe the internal ring test (deep ring occlusion test).
cards.back: The hernia is reduced with the patient supine and knees flexed; the deep ring is occluded by the thumb and the patient stands and coughs. An oblique hernia is controlled and appears only on release, whereas a direct hernia still bulges forwards through the posterior wall.

cards.front: In which direction do the contents of an oblique inguinal hernia descend and reduce?
cards.back: They descend downwards, forwards and medially, and reduce obliquely upwards, backwards and laterally - the reverse of the canal's direction.

cards.front: What shape distinguishes an oblique from a direct hernia on inspection?
cards.back: The oblique hernia is oblong with a narrow neck and wide fundus and descends along the cord; the direct hernia is globular, appears straight forwards and disappears straight backwards.

cards.front: What is a pantaloon (saddle-bag) hernia?
cards.back: Simultaneous direct and indirect sacs on the same side straddling the inferior epigastric vessels like the legs of a pair of trousers.

cards.front: What is a sliding hernia (hernia en glissade)?
cards.back: A hernia in which a retroperitoneal viscus forms part of the wall of the sac - sigmoid colon on the left, caecum on the right, or the bladder medially. The posterior wall of the sac must not be opened or excised.

cards.front: What is a Richter's hernia and where is it most common?
cards.back: Herniation of only part of the circumference of the bowel wall through a narrow ring, most often at the femoral ring. It strangulates and becomes gangrenous while the lumen remains patent, so there is no intestinal obstruction.

cards.front: What is a Littre's hernia?
cards.back: A hernia whose sac contains a Meckel's diverticulum.

cards.front: What is a Maydl's hernia?
cards.back: A W-shaped loop hernia in which two loops lie in the sac and the intervening loop remains in the abdomen. The strangulated segment is the intra-abdominal one, so it will be missed unless the loop is drawn out and inspected.

cards.front: What is an Amyand's hernia?
cards.back: An inguinal hernia whose sac contains the appendix, which may be normal or inflamed.

cards.front: How does an obturator hernia present and what is Howship-Romberg sign?
cards.back: It passes through the obturator canal, typically in a thin elderly woman, and presents as bowel obstruction with few local signs. Howship-Romberg sign is pain along the medial thigh to the knee from pressure on the obturator nerve, worsened by extension, abduction and medial rotation of the hip.

cards.front: Which structures does a hernial sac consist of, and which viscus can never be a content?
cards.back: The sac has a mouth, neck, body and fundus. Any abdominal viscus may be a content except the pancreas.

cards.front: What is the femoral sheath and what is it derived from?
cards.back: A funnel of fascia carried down behind the inguinal ligament around the femoral vessels, its anterior wall from the fascia transversalis and its posterior wall from the fascia iliaca.

cards.front: Name the three compartments of the femoral sheath from lateral to medial.
cards.back: The lateral compartment for the femoral artery, the intermediate for the femoral vein, and the medial compartment which is the femoral canal.

cards.front: Why does the femoral canal exist at all?
cards.back: It is a dead space that allows the femoral vein to expand when venous return increases; it contains fat, lymphatics and the node of Cloquet.

cards.front: Give the four boundaries of the femoral ring.
cards.back: Anteriorly the inguinal ligament, posteriorly the pectineal ligament and superior pubic ramus with pectineus, medially the sharp edge of the lacunar ligament, and laterally the femoral vein.

cards.front: Trace the course of a femoral hernia.
cards.back: Through the femoral ring into the femoral canal, down the canal to the saphenous opening, then forwards through the cribriform fascia and upwards over the inguinal ligament - so it presents below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and may then turn up over the ligament.

cards.front: Why does a femoral hernia strangulate so readily?
cards.back: Its neck at the femoral ring is narrow and is bounded on three sides by rigid structures - the inguinal ligament, the lacunar ligament and the pectineal ligament - so the contents are quickly constricted.

cards.front: Why is a femoral hernia commoner in women?
cards.back: The female pelvis is wider and the femoral ring and canal are correspondingly wider, and the fascia is stretched further by pregnancy.

cards.front: What is the corona mortis and why is it named so?
cards.back: An abnormal or enlarged obturator artery, or a large communication between the obturator and inferior epigastric or external iliac vessels, crossing the superior pubic ramus close to the lacunar ligament in about a third of people. Blind division of the lacunar ligament can tear it, giving torrential and difficult-to-control bleeding - the crown of death.

cards.front: How should the constricting ring of a strangulated femoral hernia be released safely?
cards.back: By dividing the lacunar ligament medially under direct vision with a finger or grooved director protecting the contents, having anticipated an aberrant obturator artery; some surgeons prefer to divide the inguinal ligament instead.

cards.front: Which node lies in the femoral canal and what is its significance?
cards.back: The node of Cloquet or Rosenmuller. It receives lymph from the deep inguinal chain and the glans, and an enlarged node here is a common differential diagnosis for a femoral hernia.

cards.front: Where is the saphenous opening and what covers it?
cards.back: In the fascia lata about 4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, covered by the sieve-like cribriform fascia and pierced by the great saphenous vein.

cards.front: Which surgical approaches are used for a femoral hernia?
cards.back: The low (Lockwood) approach below the inguinal ligament for elective repair, the high (McEvedy) approach through the rectus sheath for strangulation because it allows bowel resection, and the trans-inguinal (Lotheissen) approach through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

cards.front: Which structures form the femoral triangle and what is the arrangement of its contents?
cards.back: Bounded by the inguinal ligament, sartorius and adductor longus, with iliopsoas and pectineus in the floor. From lateral to medial the contents run nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics - NAVEL.

cards.front: What is the anatomical principle of a Bassini repair?
cards.back: The conjoint tendon is sutured to the in-rolled edge of the inguinal ligament behind the cord, reconstituting the posterior wall of the canal - a tension repair now largely replaced by mesh.

cards.front: What is the anatomical principle of a Shouldice repair?
cards.back: The transversalis fascia is incised and double-breasted in overlapping layers, then the conjoint tendon is approximated to the inguinal ligament, reconstructing the posterior wall and reforming a snug deep ring.

cards.front: What is the anatomical principle of a McVay repair, and which hernia is it best suited to?
cards.back: The transversus arch is sutured to the pectineal ligament of Cooper with a relaxing incision in the anterior rectus sheath. Because it closes the femoral ring as well, it suits femoral and large direct hernias.

cards.front: What is the anatomical principle of a Lichtenstein repair?
cards.back: A flat mesh is laid tension-free over the whole posterior wall from the pubic tubercle to beyond the deep ring, overlapping the internal oblique, with its tails split around the cord to recreate a snug deep ring.

cards.front: Define the triangle of doom in laparoscopic hernia repair.
cards.back: Bounded medially by the vas deferens and laterally by the gonadal vessels, with the external iliac vessels in its floor. No tack or staple may be placed within it.

cards.front: Define the triangle of pain in laparoscopic hernia repair.
cards.back: Bounded medially by the gonadal vessels and laterally and superiorly by the iliopubic tract, containing the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the femoral nerve. Fixation here causes neuralgia.

cards.front: What is herniotomy and for whom is it sufficient?
cards.back: Excision of the sac alone after transfixion at its neck. In infants and children the wall is otherwise normal and herniotomy alone cures the hernia.

cards.front: Distinguish herniorrhaphy from hernioplasty.
cards.back: Herniorrhaphy strengthens the posterior wall using the patient's own tissues after herniotomy; hernioplasty reinforces it with a prosthetic mesh without tension.

cards.front: What is the iliopubic tract and why do laparoscopic surgeons use it as a landmark?
cards.back: A thickened band of transversalis fascia running parallel and deep to the inguinal ligament from the iliopectineal arch to the pubic tubercle. Seen from inside the abdomen it is the visible inferior landmark for the deep ring, and no tack should be placed below it laterally.

cards.front: What is the shelving edge of the inguinal ligament?
cards.back: The in-rolled posterior part of the ligament that faces upwards and backwards; it is the tissue into which the conjoint tendon is sutured in a Bassini repair and to which mesh is anchored inferiorly.

cards.front: What is the reflected part of the inguinal ligament (Colles' ligament)?
cards.back: Fibres from the medial end of the inguinal ligament that turn upwards behind the superficial ring towards the linea alba, reinforcing the posterior wall behind the ring.

cards.front: What structures does the transversalis fascia sling contribute to the deep ring, and what does it do?
cards.back: Its upper and lower crura form a U-shaped sling open above and medially; contraction of transversus abdominis pulls the sling upwards and laterally, tightening the ring around the cord.

cards.front: How does the Nyhus classification describe groin hernias anatomically?
cards.back: Type 1 is an indirect hernia with a normal deep ring, type 2 an indirect hernia with a dilated ring but an intact posterior wall, type 3 a posterior wall defect subdivided into direct (3a), indirect with a destroyed posterior wall (3b) and femoral (3c), and type 4 a recurrent hernia.

cards.front: Define the four clinical stages a hernia may pass through.
cards.back: Reducible, irreducible (incarcerated) where contents cannot be returned but the blood supply is intact, obstructed where the lumen is occluded but the supply is preserved, and strangulated where the blood supply is cut off.

cards.front: Where does strangulation of a hernia usually begin and in what order do the tissues die?
cards.back: At the ring of constriction, most often the neck of the sac or a rigid ring such as the superficial ring, deep ring or femoral ring. Venous return is obstructed first, then arterial inflow; the bowel becomes congested, then purple, then black and finally perforates, with peritonitis as the terminal event.

cards.front: What is an inflamed hernia and how does it differ from a strangulated one?
cards.back: One in which the contents are inflamed from within, as in appendicitis or salpingitis in the sac. It is tender but the skin is red and the systemic upset relates to the inflamed organ, whereas strangulation gives severe pain, absent cough impulse and rapid toxicity.

cards.front: What is an interstitial hernia?
cards.back: A hernia whose sac lies between the layers of the abdominal wall rather than emerging subcutaneously - preperitoneal, interparietal between the muscle layers, or superficial deep to the external oblique. It presents with obstruction and no visible lump.

cards.front: Why does a sliding hernia commonly contain the bladder medially, and what warns of it?
cards.back: The bladder is extraperitoneal and lies adjacent to the medial end of the canal, so it can be drawn into the medial wall of a direct sac. A history of two-stage micturition or of needing to compress the lump to empty the bladder warns of it, and inadvertent cystotomy is the penalty.

cards.front: How long is the femoral canal and what is the anatomy of its lower end?
cards.back: About 1.25 cm long, ending at the saphenous opening where the cribriform fascia closes it; the hernia must therefore turn forwards and then upwards, which gives it its characteristic retort shape.

cards.front: Which four structures pass beneath the inguinal ligament in the lacuna musculorum and lacuna vasorum?
cards.back: Laterally in the muscular compartment the iliopsoas, femoral nerve and lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh; medially in the vascular compartment the femoral artery and vein within the femoral sheath, with the femoral canal at its medial edge.

cards.front: Which structures may be mistaken for a femoral hernia?
cards.back: An enlarged node of Cloquet, a saphena varix which has a fluid thrill and disappears on lying down, a psoas abscess or bursa, a lipoma, an ectopic testis and a femoral artery aneurysm.

mcqs.stem: A strangulated femoral hernia in an obese woman requires resection of gangrenous ileum. Which approach gives the safest access to both the sac and the bowel?

options.text: Low (Lockwood) approach below the inguinal ligament
options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

options.text: Trans-inguinal (Lotheissen) approach through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal
options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

options.text: High (McEvedy) approach through the lower rectus sheath and the preperitoneal space
options.why:
Key - C) High (McEvedy) approach through the lower rectus sheath and the preperitoneal space. The high approach enters above the inguinal ligament through the lower rectus sheath into the preperitoneal space, so the ring can be released under vision and the peritoneum opened to resect and anastomose bowel.

Why the others fail:
A) Low (Lockwood) approach below the inguinal ligament - The low approach exposes the sac well but gives no room to deliver and resect bowel, and the constriction is hard to release from below.
B) Trans-inguinal (Lotheissen) approach through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal - The trans-inguinal approach destroys the posterior wall of the inguinal canal and still gives restricted access for a resection.
D) Laparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal repair - A laparoscopic repair is a poor choice in the presence of gangrenous bowel and contamination and does not allow safe resection in this setting.

mcqs.stem: Which anatomical statement best explains why a mesh repair has a lower recurrence rate than a Bassini repair for a large direct hernia?

options.text: Mesh closes the deep inguinal ring more completely
options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

options.text: Mesh replaces the deficient transversalis fascia over the whole myopectineal orifice without approximating structures that are not normally in contact
options.why:
Key - B) Mesh replaces the deficient transversalis fascia over the whole myopectineal orifice without approximating structures that are not normally in contact. The failure in a direct hernia is the transversalis fascia of the posterior wall, and a tension repair pulls the conjoint tendon down to the inguinal ligament, two structures not normally apposed, so the suture line is under permanent tension; mesh restores the whole myopectineal orifice without tension.

Why the others fail:
A) Mesh closes the deep inguinal ring more completely - Closing the deep ring is relevant to the indirect hernia; a large direct hernia arises medial to it.
C) Mesh restores the shutter mechanism of the internal oblique - No repair restores the physiological shutter action of a denervated or attenuated muscle.
D) Mesh prevents the ilioinguinal nerve from being caught in the repair - Mesh in fact raises rather than lowers the risk of nerve entrapment and chronic groin pain.
